Hi all, I'm a high school student with a background in olympiad mathematics and proofs. I've recently become interested in lean and possibly contributing. I have a few questions - is it possible for me to meaningfully contribute without taking some upper-division math courses? I've taken most of the standard lower level courses up to Calculus 3 and ODEs, and while I haven't taken a formal proof class I have had some experience with proof-based competitions such as USAMO and BAMO. If so, where would be an approrpriate place for me to begin? I've heard that formalizing proofs of competition problems is an area with a relatively low bar to contribute, and if so how/where should I begin? I also have very limited experience with cs and the whole git system but I've been told that isn't too hard to learn.

Again please forgive me if my questions seem oblivious. Really excited to see where I can go with this!

It would be difficult nowadays to contribute to Lean's mathematics library but there's plenty you can do on your own -- I started by formalising a ton of elementary bit tricky questions at Olympiad and first year undergrad level. If you actually want to learn how to use the software then I would recommend reading books such as #tpil and #mil rather than using AI -- AI can do lots of problems at this level and if you use it then you don't struggle, and struggling is when you learn. When you've struggled a bit then you're probably ready to contribute, and there are repositories which collect Olympiad style problems which would probably be happy to accept contributions

I'd recommend just learning how to use Lean, first. Just setting it up properly can be quite a challenge, as it will test your abilities to troubleshoot and fine tune both your hardware and your OS. Only once you have a stable build, can you start on the programming syntax and finally formal theorem proving.

There's a great intro game for theorem proving that is on the front pages; it's online and doesn't require a build. Very fun and gives a solid introduction to the fundamentals of number theory and type theory.

Setting up lean + mathlib is extremely easy nowadays; I have no idea what you mean by "just setting it up properly can be quite a challenge". Which parts of the clear instructions on the official Lean website are you struggling with? This message almost reads like it is AI-generated. I also don't know what you mean by "the front pages" but to the OP maybe you would be interested in the natural number game, which I wrote for 1st year undergraduates and no doubt would be in scope for you.
haha I had no idea you were the one who made the natural number game! I've been trying it for the past few hours, and it's been very entertaining!

Hello everyone i have math background of commutative algrebra and am currently extremely interested in Lean4. If you are beginner let's share growing. Please help me find right direction to contribute to lean community and verified AI development.

Well, maybe I had an interesting experience.

I started with an AI, as I was expecting to use one regardless to get me through the translational aspect (I'm not a type theory theorem prover just yet). AI's are pretty good at translating languages, whether they are human, mathematical, or computer code. Anyways, my AI told me to not use the website setup, because it was the wrong version (I dont remember the specifics, the last week has been hell), so we did a download/install through powershell using github. That went smoothly, and I did have Lean up in short order. I got probably halfway through my project in the first night, and was very pleased, and then problems began to occur. Proofs were not compiling the way they should, the library seemed to mismatch what the AI was looking for, and my computer started to crash.

I have a hell of rig, built it myself so that my handicapped son could play VR, but it couldn't handle the mathlib load. The AI was also getting lost (I learned enough to realize this now) and we ended up trying to switch builds in order to get part of the library accessible (shouldn't ever have done this), and when I got a new version in, nothing would compile at all, and my computer started crashing even more.

So I had two days of digging through my OS, fixing about a dozen bugs in windows I didn't even know existed (like path file corruption, yay), resetting my hardware timings multiple times, updating drivers, went through a period where my computer crashed every ten minutes, finally realized my load line calibration actually needed to be way higher than standard due to my rig, got stability, and after all of that, I used the website to reinstall Lean. And it stuck me on the experimental toolchain. ..

Im writing a formal proof for a major submission, and I really really did not want to be on the experimental branch, i wanted 4.29 or whatever its called, the last stable version. (maybe this is also a mistake? I dont know) So that was another day figuring out why in the hell lake kept reverting to experimental, no matter how many wipes and overrides and resets I did.

In the end of it all, I got my version to work, I got my project reconnected, and I learned a WHOLE lot about how everything works. I definitely wasted a lot of time (and sleep), and it was easily one of the hardest things I've been through in my academic career. But I learned. I think I could install lean with my eyes closed at this point, and I am definitely, definitely switching to Linux.

So yeah. That happened. I didn't mean to be disrespectful, clearly it sounds like I didn't have the normal experience. I am very, very happy to have Lean and very grateful for all the work you and your colleagues have put into it.

I still stand by my point: that its a good idea to learn how to install it, learn about your hardware and software limitations (building mathlib is actually infamous among gamers and over clocking experts as a true stress test, cinebench doesnt even come close), and just begin to learn to use Lean and Lake from the ground up, before going in and trying to contribute to mathlib. I know its a community effort and everything is essentially peer-reviewed AND type-checked, but I can't imagine being part of that group without having a somewhat strong grasp of the platform.

But yeah, ok... what do I know? :) Was just my two cents from one beginner to another.
And I also meant your number theory game, theres a link to it in the beginning of the Lean webpage (the front pages). Its a great game.
I see. So you didn't follow the instructions, followed what the AI said, got in a mess, and then claimed that it was difficult to install. I guess that's one way of doing it!

Anyhow, I feel bad that this thread has been so thoroughly derailed, so this is my last post here.
I am pretty sure Lean has been multithreaded for a while

@Daniel Liao I recall that Mathlib does not contain a lot of results in euclidean / projective geometry, which is something you could probably try to formalize if you have olympiad maths experience.
But it will also be quite challanging for the beginning, I guess, and I don't know if it is even something that would fit into Mathlib because it is not really relevant for higher maths.

I have once taken a formalization course in university and in order to earn credits for it, students had to do a formalization project of something that is not already in Mathlib and some of the suggestions of my professor included Menelaos' Theorem, Desargues' Theorem and Pascal's Theorem. I attempted to formalize Desargues' Theorem, but got stuck since there was not really a framework for projective geometry (there is a notion of projective spaces, but not enough specific results for RP^2), so I ended up doing a different formalization project instead.
This preprint may be of interest for Euclidean geometry autoformalisation :)
